Q: Can buffers or constant sized external arrays be used to create an fully in place iterative quicksort? A:

'that both take up n log n stack space': no they don't. Quicksort needs 'at most lg N', or in exercise 20 max(0,lg (N+2)/(M+2)). - Knuth, D.E., The Art of Computer Programming, vol 2 #5.2.2.

Q: Refreshing error stating Memory not enough in Power BI A:

If you are running Power BI 32-bit (click "File" and then "About" in desktop to find out), then I would suggest uninstalling and installing a 64-bit version.

Another potential fix is to head to "Data Cache Management Options", clear cache or increase the "maximum allowed" figure.

Q: Hadoop: There are 0 datanode(s) running and no node(s) are excluded in this operation A:

Q: What is the difference between MOV and LEA? A:

None of the existing answers quite got to the bottom of my own confusion, so I'd like to add my own.

What I was missing is that lea operations treat the use of parentheses different than how mov operations do.

Think of C. Let's say I have an array of long that I call array. The expression array[i] loads the value from memory at address array + i[1].

On the other hand, consider &array[i]: this still contains the text array[i], but no memory lookup is performed! The meaning of array[i] has changed. It now acts as a kind of a specification, telling & what memory address we're looking for, without asking for it to be loaded.

The situation is analogous with mov and lea. With mov, a memory load occurs that does not happen with lea, despite both instructions using parentheses.

For instance, consider movq (%rdi, %rsi, 8), %rbp. This computes the address %rdi + %rsi * 8, loads the value at that address, and stores the loaded result into %rbp.

Contrast with leaq (%rdi, %rsi, 8), %rbp: this computes the value %rdi + %si * 8 (same value as before!), but does not load it. Instead, it places that value directly into %rbp. No load from memory is involved, just arithmetic operations[2].

[1] Note that when C sees array + i it actually computes array plus i × sizeof(long), automatically scaling the increment i by the whatever type your array contains. This is so that you can just write + i to mean "ith element"!

[2] Side note: because lea only does arithmetic operations, its arguments don't have to be valid addresses. Accordingly, it can be used to perform arithmetic on values that aren't intended to be deferenced at all. For instance, cc with -O2 optimization translates

long f(long x) {
  return x * 5;
}

into the following (irrelevant lines removed):

f:
  leaq (%rdi, %rdi, 4), %rax  # set %rax to %rdi + %rdi * 4
  ret
